In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in [[geometric measure theory]] &mdash; a '''uniformly distributed measure''' on a [[metric space]] is one for which the measure of an [[open ball]] depends only on its radius and not on its centre.  By convention, the measure is also required to be [[Borel regular measure|Borel regular]], and to take positive and finite values on open balls of finite radius.  Thus, if (''X'',&nbsp;''d'') is a metric space, a Borel regular measure ''&mu;'' on ''X'' is said to be '''uniformly distributed''' if
:<math>0 < \mu(\mathbf{B}_{r}(x)) = \mu(\mathbf{B}_{r}(y)) < + \infty</math>
for all points ''x'' and ''y'' of ''X'' and all 0&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;''r''&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;+&infin;, where
:<math>\mathbf{B}_{r}(x) := \{ z \in X | d(x, z) < r \}.</math>

==Christensen's lemma==

As it turns out, uniformly distributed measures are very rigid objects.  On any "decent" metric space, the uniformly distributed measures form a one-parameter linearly dependent family:

Let ''&mu;'' and ''&nu;'' be uniformly distributed Borel regular measures on a [[separable space|separable]] metric space (''X'',&nbsp;''d'').  Then there is a constant ''c'' such that ''&mu;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''c&nu;''.
